chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah from 'Ammar al-Sabati who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a woman who is among the people of a house (i.e., under the guardianship of a male relative) and she dislikes for the people of her house to know about it. Is it permissible for her to appoint a man who wishes to marry her, saying to him, 'I have appointed you, so witness my marriage to you'? He said: No. I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, and if she is a virgin (ayyim)?' He said: And if she is a virgin. I said: And if she appoints someone else to marry her to him, will he marry her to him? He said: Yes. The reason in this report is that it was not permissible because she appointed him to marry her to himself, and that is not valid because the agent stands in the place of the principal, so he needs someone to contract on his behalf, and it is not valid for a person to contract on himself because the contract requires offer and acceptance, and that is not valid between a person and himself. And if she married herself to him without appointing him, that would be permissible according to what the earlier reports contained. And for the reason we mentioned, the questioner said to him: 'She appoints someone else to marry her to him?' He said: Yes, because that is valid to be estimated in him, and in the first case it is not valid, and it adds clarity to what we have presented.

key_terms.أَيَّماً: virgin (one who has not been married)

ai.seo_question: Can a woman appoint a suitor as her agent to marry her to himself in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the juristic nuance of a woman appointing a suitor as her agent to marry her to himself, ruling it invalid due to the logical impossibility of one person simultaneously holding the roles of offeror and acceptor in the contract. The Imam distinguishes this from appointing a third party, which is permissible, thereby resolving apparent contradictions in earlier reports regarding a widow's right to contract her own marriage. This explanation underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise legal mechanics (*usul al-fiqh*) within the *fiqh* of marriage.
